title: Sammy Gravano
wiki_lead:
Salvatore "Sammy the Bull" Gravano (born March 12, 1945) is an American former mobster who rose to the position of underboss in the Gambino crime family of New York City before becoming a government witness. As the underboss, Gravano played a major role in prosecuting John Gotti, the crime family's boss, by agreeing to testify as a government witness against him and other mobsters in a deal. As part of the agreement, Gravano confessed to his involvement in at least 19 murders, although he was also responsible for a number of other crimes.
Originally an associate for the Colombo crime family, and later for the Brooklyn faction of the Gambino family, Gravano was part of the group in 1985 that conspired to murder Gambino boss Paul Castellano. Gravano played a key role in planning and executing Castellano's murder, along with John Gotti, Angelo Ruggiero, Frank DeCicco, and Joseph Armone.
Soon after Castellano's murder, Gotti elevated Gravano to become an official captain after Salvatore "Toddo" Aurelio stepped down, a position Gravano held until 1987 when he became consigliere. In 1988, he became underboss, a position he held at the time he became a government witness. In 1991, Gravano agreed to turn state's evidence and testify for the prosecution against Gotti after hearing the boss making several disparaging and untrue remarks about Gravano on a wiretap that implicated them both in several murders.
At the time, Gravano was among the highest-ranking members of the Five Families to break his blood oath and to cooperate with the government. As a result of his testimonies, Gotti and Frank LoCascio were sentenced to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole in 1992. In 1994, a federal judge sentenced Gravano to five years in prison; however, since Gravano had already served four years, the sentence amounted to less than one year. He was released early and entered the U.S. federal Witness Protection Program in Colorado, but left the program in 1995 after eight months and moved to Arizona with his family.
In 1997, Gravano was consulted several times for the biographical book about his life, Underboss, by author Peter Maas. In February 2000, Gravano and nearly 40 other ring members—including his wife Debra, daughter Karen and son Gerard—were arrested on federal and state drug charges.
In 2001, Gravano and his son, Gerard, were indicted on mirror charges with the federal government. In 2002, Gravano was sentenced in New York to twenty years in prison. A month later, he was also sentenced in Arizona to nineteen years in prison to run concurrently. Additionally, Gravano was sentenced to lifetime supervised release and a $100,000 fine. He was released in September 2017.
On the day of his sentencing in 1994, federal authorities stated as a result of Gravano's testimony, there had been "37 convictions, nine people awaiting trial, eight people resigned from the unions as a result of Gravano's cooperation." They also said that Gravano was indirectly responsible for even more convictions, as his actions had encouraged others to become witnesses against the Mafia.

grok_lead: Salvatore "Sammy the Bull" Gravano (born March 12, 1945) is an American former mobster who rose to become underboss of the Gambino crime family in New York City before turning state's witness in 1991, providing testimony that led to the conviction of boss John Gotti on murder and racketeering charges. Admitting involvement in 19 murders during his Mafia career, Gravano received a reduced five-year prison sentence for his cooperation; after credit for time served, he was released in 1994 and entered witness protection. He later violated the terms of his deal by leading an ecstasy trafficking ring in Arizona, resulting in a 20-year sentence in 2002 and release in 2017. As of 2026, Gravano resides in the Phoenix area, where he hosts the podcast Our Thing and participates in media projects discussing his past, including a biographical film in development at Amblin Entertainment with a screenplay by Nick Pileggi. Born in the Bensonhurst neighborhood of Brooklyn, New York, to Italian-American parents, Gravano grew up in a tight-knit community marked by poverty and street violence. Struggling with severe dyslexia, he dropped out of school at age 16 and began engaging in petty crimes such as shoplifting and burglary, leading to his first arrest at 18. He joined the Rampers street gang in his early teens and later served two years in the U.S. Army during the Vietnam War era, receiving an honorable discharge in 1966. Upon returning to Brooklyn, Gravano entered organized crime, initially associating with the Colombo crime family in 1968 before switching allegiance to the Gambinos in the early 1970s. Gravano's ascent in the Gambino family was rapid and ruthless; he was formally inducted as a made man in 1975 and committed his first murder in 1970, eventually rising to captain, consigliere, and underboss by the mid-1980s under bosses like Paul Castellano and John Gotti. His criminal enterprises included extortion, loan-sharking, construction racketeering, gambling, and union corruption, generating millions in illicit revenue while he personally orchestrated or participated in numerous hits, including the 1985 assassination of Castellano that paved the way for Gotti's leadership. Despite his violent reputation, Gravano portrayed himself as a devoted family man in his 1997 memoir Underboss, co-authored with Peter Maas, emphasizing his preference for quiet evenings at home over the excesses of some mob figures. His decision to flip stemmed from Gotti's betrayal during their 1990 trial and a desire for a legitimate future for his children, leading to unprecedented testimony that dismantled much of the family's leadership. After his initial release, Gravano relocated to Arizona under witness protection but abandoned the program to pursue business ventures, culminating in his 2000 arrest for distributing over 40,000 ecstasy pills through a network involving his son Gerard. The operation highlighted his inability to fully sever ties to crime, resulting in the seizure of book royalties and assets to compensate victims' families. Post-2017, Gravano has embraced public life, producing content like YouTube videos and documentaries that recount Mafia lore, including a 2025 Max special on his drug ring, while commenting on contemporary issues like sports betting scandals from his Phoenix home. His story remains a defining chapter in American organized crime history, illustrating both the allure and downfall of the Mafia subculture.
